items.title: Katseye Drops Out of Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields Festival: ‘It Breaks Our Hearts’
items.summary:
Katseye has withdrawn from Olivia Rodrigo's Daisy Chain Fields Festival, the one-day event set for Saturday in Irvine, California. The group announced the decision in a note posted to its social media accounts, pointing to an ankle injury sustained by member Megan Skiendiel.

"Megan sprained her ankle yesterday during tour rehearsal and after being evaluated by doctors, she has been advised to stay off it and allow it to properly heal so we can be ready for our upcoming tour," the statement read. The group added that "it breaks our hearts to disappoint anyone who made plans to be there," and singled out the festival's charitable framing as a reason it had been looking forward to the booking.

Katseye had been scheduled to play the Dandelion Stage at 2:15 p.m., slotted between Santigold and Mitski. Variety reported that festival organizers issued a revised schedule in which Santigold takes over the vacated time slot.

The timing is awkward for the group, which begins its Wildworld tour in Dublin on September 1. Dates run through the U.K. and Europe into mid-September before the tour moves to North America in October. Neither the group nor its representatives have said what, if anything, the injury means for that schedule.

The withdrawal comes during the strongest commercial stretch of Katseye's career to date. The group recently landed its first No. 1 album on the Billboard 200 with Wild. In its note, the group said it was "sending all our love to Olivia and to all of the incredible artists, non-profit organizations and volunteers who have given their time to make this day so special."

items.title: David Byrne’s Dazzling Tour Being Turned Into a Film by ‘Brutalist’ Director Brady Corbet, Shooting in 70mm
items.summary:
Brady Corbet, the director of The Brutalist, has shot a concert film built around David Byrne's Who Is the Sky? tour and is now in postproduction on it. The movie was filmed over multiple nights at the Hippodrome in Baltimore, Byrne's hometown, using a combination of 8-perf and 15-perf 70mm.

Variety reported the project, noting that no distributor or release date has been set, and that Byrne's film agents at the Gersh Agency are handling global rights along with producer The Deep End Films. Records show the Baltimore shows took place in May, with attendees noting on social media at the time that a camera crew was present.

Byrne said the format choice surprised him. "When Brady told me he wanted to shoot our show in 70 millimeter (70 millimeter!) I didn't realize what a difference it would make until I saw some frames he sent me," he said in a statement. "He was right, it really does capture the widescreen visual scope of the show. I've never seen anything like it."

Corbet framed the film around its setting. "The band's performance is an inclusive celebration of community, and of Baltimore in particular — one of America's most underappreciated historic cities," he said. The Deep End produces with Corbet's company Pre-Code and Mona Fastvold, presented by River Road Entertainment; producers include Amit Dey, Jason Fine, Corbet, Maddie Browning and Byrne, with River Road's Bill Pohlad among the executive producers.

The film continues a run of directors drawn to Byrne's stage work, following Jonathan Demme's Stop Making Sense with Talking Heads and Spike Lee's American Utopia six years ago. The Deep End's recent music titles include Sly Lives!, The Sparks Brothers and Little Richard: I Am Everything. Corbet's next project, Origin of the World, shoots later this year with Cate Blanchett, Michael Fassbender and Selena Gomez.

Byrne is in the final stretch of a tour that began last September. After a November run at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood, he returns to Los Angeles for two nights at the Hollywood Bowl on Friday and Saturday, followed by five shows in Mexico and a closing date September 19 at Forest Hills Stadium in Queens.

items.title: Ellen Pompeo To Star In ‘Not A Sound’ Drama In Works At Hulu From David E. Kelley Productions
items.summary:
Ellen Pompeo and David E. Kelley are developing a drama together for the first time. Hulu has set up Not a Sound for development through 20th Television, with Pompeo attached to star as a nurse who loses her hearing in a hit-and-run.

In the project, disgraced ER nurse Amelia Winn and her service dog discover the body of a murdered former colleague, a death that pulls her into a mystery tied to the accident that cost her her hearing. Deadline reported the setup, which is based on Heather Gudenkauf's novel of the same name. Azazel Jacobs, who wrote and directed His Three Daughters, is set to direct.

David E. Kelley Productions president Matthew Tinker and Annakate Chappell wrote the script. The two previously worked together as writers on Kelley's ABC drama Big Sky. Chappell executive produces alongside Jacobs, Kelley, Tinker, and Pompeo and Laura Holstein of Calamity Jane. 20th Television is the studio.

The pairing carries a bit of scheduling history. In March 2005, Kelley's Boston Legal wrapped its season in ABC's Sunday 10 p.m. slot to clear room for Grey's Anatomy, which launched in the same hour a week later with Pompeo as Meredith Grey.

Pompeo is under an overall deal at 20th Television and has been busy there. Hulu recently ordered a second season of the anthology Good American Family, which she executive produces, and greenlit the dramedy pilot Chicks, in which she stars and executive produces, both with Katie Robbins. She also stars in and executive produces Grey's Anatomy, heading into its 23rd season, and is an executive producer on a West Texas–set spinoff due in midseason 2027.

Jacobs won Gotham and Independent Spirit awards for the His Three Daughters screenplay and directed both seasons of Doll & Em for Sky and HBO. Tinker's producing slate includes second seasons of Presumed Innocent and Margo's Got Money Troubles for Apple TV and Netflix's Myron Bolitar. Not a Sound remains in development, with no order announced.

items.title: André “3000” Benjamin & Cathy Moriarty Join ‘Scooby-Doo: Origins’ Netflix Series Cast
items.summary:
André 3000 Benjamin and Cathy Moriarty have joined the cast of Scooby-Doo: Origins, Netflix's live-action series based on the Hanna-Barbera property. Both will appear in recurring roles. Deadline reported the casting, noting the show is shooting in Atlanta for a 2027 global release.

For Benjamin, the job is a return to the franchise by an unusual route. He and Big Boi, as OutKast, co-wrote "Land of a Million Drums" with Killer Mike and Sleepy Brown for the 2002 Scooby-Doo movie, which produced a sequel in 2004. That film remains the only previous live-action take on the cartoon.

The series casts Mckenna Grace as Daphne Blake, Tanner Hagen as Shaggy Rogers, Abby Ryder Fortson as Velma Dinkley and Maxwell Jenkins as Fred Jones. The supporting ensemble already includes Paul Walter Hauser, Sara Gilbert, Bruce McGill, Peter Macon, Rusty Schwimmer, Jona Xiao and Wynn Everett, among others.

The story is set during the group's final summer at camp, where Shaggy and Daphne become entangled in a mystery involving a lost Great Dane puppy that may have witnessed a supernatural murder. Velma, a scientifically minded local, and Freddy, the new kid in town, join the case as it starts exposing each character's secrets.

Josh Appelbaum and Scott Rosenberg serve as showrunners, writers and executive producers. Greg Berlanti, Sarah Schechter and Leigh London Redman executive produce through Berlanti Productions and its overall deal with Warner Bros. Television, alongside Midnight Radio's André Nemec, Jeff Pinkner and Adrienne Erickson, and Toby Haynes, who directed the first episode. Warner Bros. Television is the studio.

Benjamin played Jimi Hendrix in the 2013 film Jimi: All Is by My Side, earning an Independent Spirit Award nomination, and has appeared in Four Brothers, High Life and White Noise. Moriarty was Oscar-nominated for Raging Bull and starred in 1998's Casper, with recent guest turns on Will Trent and Elsbeth.

items.title: Tupac Murder Trial Testimony Ends With Cop Saying He Was Told to ‘Stand Down’ on Keffe D Arrest
items.summary:
Duane "Keffe D" Davis rested his defense Thursday in the Las Vegas murder trial over the 1996 drive-by shooting of Tupac Shakur, calling three witnesses in under two hours. Closing arguments are scheduled for Monday.

All three witnesses were former Las Vegas Metropolitan Police officers, and defense attorney Michael Sanft used them to build toward reasonable doubt. Former Sgt. Stan Hyt and former Lt. Charlie Mangrum testified they were working overtime that night, watching the home of Death Row Records co-founder Suge Knight, who was expected to host a party after Mike Tyson's bout at the MGM Grand. Both said they saw a light-colored Cadillac arrive and later depart in a convoy that included Knight driving Shakur in his BMW.

The detail matters because witnesses told police that a light-colored Cadillac pulled alongside Knight's BMW less than an hour later, and that someone in the back seat opened fire. Prosecutors allege Davis, a leader of the South Side Compton Crips, rode in the front passenger seat of a rented white Cadillac and let his nephew Orlando Anderson shoot at the BMW in retaliation for an attack on Anderson inside the MGM Grand.

Under cross-examination by Clark County Chief Deputy District Attorney Marc DiGiacomo, Mangrum said his report that night logged the license plates of every vehicle entering Knight's property, and agreed that 1996 homicide detectives would have followed up on that information. Rolling Stone, citing a Law & Crime trial livestream, reported the exchange.

The defense's final witness was former homicide Det. Dan Long, who ran the Shakur investigation from 2002 to 2017. Long testified that the paper case file had to be locked down because department employees were accessing it out of curiosity, and that some of his reports disappeared when the department changed electronic storage systems. Sanft also pressed him on a 2009 interview he conducted with Davis in Los Angeles.

At the center of the case is a December 2008 proffer session with LAPD and federal investigators, in which Davis said he sat in the Cadillac's front passenger seat and handed a loaded .40-caliber Glock to the men behind him. Prosecutors say Davis forfeited the limited protections attached to that statement by repeating the details publicly, including in a BET docuseries and his 2019 memoir Compton Street Legend. Sanft has told jurors Davis invented the account for leverage in a drug investigation and later for money: "It's because they knew he was full of crap."
